docs.title: Welcome to MAE4001
docs.text:
Convergent Media and Users

Welcome to MAE4001: Convergent Media and Users! This course is taught by Dr. MJ Rheu (유민진) at Sogang University, based in Seoul, South Korea.

Communication technologies powerfully shape how we attend, learn, communicate, make decisions, and relate to others. Their impact is not accidental: although it may be difficult to discern, it is a product of careful and deliberate design based on decades of socio-psychological research findings.

This course aims to help students understand how socio-psychological mechanisms and technological affordances shape user experiences across converging media. Its premise is that communication technologies are not neutral containers: they embody assumptions about users and translate psychological principles into designed features that can influence attention, emotion, relationships, and behavior. Through a project-based process, students will move from user research and theoretical explanation to a responsible, functional design response.

Syllabus Weekly Plans Class Project Overview From understanding a user problem to developing a theory-informed design response.

docs.title: Class Project: User Research and Technology Design
docs.text:
In this class project, your team will experience a theory-informed communication technology design process. This project comprises of three project stages, where different in-class activities are housed. Across these stages, you will identify a meaningful user problem, investigate the experiences and needs of intended users, connect user evidence and socio-psychological theories to develop a technology-based response, and create and evaluate a functional prototype. You will submit three project deliverables on Weeks 7, 11, and 16 and do the final presentation at the end of the semester.

The project follows the Double Diamond method: Discover and Define the user problem, then Develop and Deliver a design response.

docs.title: General Requirements
docs.text:
1. Note that your project deliverables are not conventional prose reports. They may combine concise written explanations with research, design artifacts, prototypes, and other materials specified in the instructions.
  2. Follow the specific generative-AI boundaries stated in each deliverable's instructions. Disclose AI use as required and take responsibility for all submitted claims, design decisions, content, and code.
  3. Make sure to always cite research and other external sources using the format required in class.
  4. Requests for deadline extensions must be communicated in advance and supported by reasons recognized under university policy.

docs.title: Project Stage 1: User Research and Problem Definition
Goals
docs.text:
In this stage, your team will discover and define a meaningful user problem before proposing a technological solution. The problem may be a recurring inconvenience in everyday life or a more consequential social challenge, such as loneliness and social isolation among older adults or difficulties experienced by young job seekers. In either case, your team should be able to explain why it is socially important and meaningful to address the problem for the intended users. In this stage, you will do the following:

  1. Identify a problem space and intended users
    • Begin with observations of everyday life and identify a user group, context, and problem worth investigating.
    • Frame the problem without assuming that technology is necessarily the solution.
  2. Gather and synthesize user evidence
    • Conduct background research and interview intended users to understand both the broader context of the problem and their lived experiences.
    • Organize the evidence to identify user needs, recurring patterns, and important insights using a design-thinking method.
  3. Define the user problem
    • Use the synthesized user evidence to develop a POV (point of view) statement and How Might We question.

docs.title: In-Class Activities
docs.text:
The following in-class activities will guide you through this stage:

  1. Week 2: Problem Discovery and Team Selection
  2. Week 3: User Interview Planning
  3. Week 5: Affinity Mapping and Problem Definition

docs.title: Deliverable #1: User Research and Problem Definition Brief
docs.text: Due by Week 7. Detailed instructions and evaluation criteria will be provided separately.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
In this stage, your team will move from defining the user problem to developing a theory-informed technological response. You will use insights about the users and relevant psychological theories to generate solution concepts, select an appropriate technological medium, and develop interface features intended to address the defined problem.

  1. Develop theory-informed solution concepts

    • Identify psychological theories or mechanisms that offer useful insights into the intended users and their experiences.
    • Generate and compare multiple solution concepts before selecting a concept and technological medium.
    • Translate the relevant theoretical insights into an interface design strategy.

  2. Develop a user scenario and critical task flow

    • Create a concrete scenario showing when, why, and how an intended user would engage with the proposed technology.
    • Identify one critical user pathway that the functional prototype will demonstrate.

docs.title: In-Class Activities
docs.text:
1. Week 9: Design Concept Studio
  2. Week 10: User Scenario and Task Flow

docs.title: Deliverable #2: Theory-Based Design Proposal
docs.text: Due by Week 11. Detailed instructions and evaluation criteria will be provided separately.

docs.title: Project Stage 3: Prototyping, Evaluation, and Revision
Goals
docs.text:
In this stage, your team will give concrete form to the design of your proposed technological solution, exchange peer feedback, and revise the proposed design and revise it using peer feedback. The goal is not to build a complete product, but rather to materialize the design idea, and discover interaction problems as well as unintended issues that may not have been visible or expected during the previous stages.

  1. Develop and critique a low-fidelity prototype

    • Translate the critical task flow into a low-fidelity representation of main features.
    • Use design critique to identify unclear interactions and improve the pathway.
    • Gather peer feedback to identify problems and make revision decisions.

  2. Create a functional prototype

    • Build a focused, workable implementation of the critical user pathway based on the peer feedback.

docs.title: In-Class Activities
docs.text:
1. Week 11: Low-Fidelity Prototyping and Critique
  2. Week 12: Functional Prototyping Studio

docs.title: Deliverable #3: Functional Prototype and Design Case
docs.text: Due by Week 16. Detailed instructions and evaluation criteria will be provided separately.

docs.title: Final Presentation and Individual Accountability
docs.text:
Each team will present its user problem, design rationale, functional prototype, and major learning from the development and evaluation process. Presentation requirements will be provided separately.

Each student will also submit an individual contribution statement and a confidential peer evaluation. These may be used to adjust individual grades when there is evidence of substantially unequal participation.

docs.title: Ⅰ. Course Overview
docs.text:
Communication technologies powerfully shape how we attend, learn, communicate, make decisions, and relate to others. Their impact is not accidental: although it may be difficult to discern, it is a product of careful and deliberate design based on decades of socio-psychological research findings.

This course aims to open your eyes to the social-psychological mechanisms and technological affordances underlying user experiences across various media, including social media, mobile apps, games, VR, and AI-powered technologies. These technologies increasingly converge, allowing users to navigate an interconnected media landscape rather than engaging with each in isolation. Understanding users in this environment requires attention both to the distinctive affordances of each medium and to the psychological principles that operate across media boundaries.

The course follows a project-based, learning-by-doing model. Using design-thinking methods, students will identify a meaningful user problem, gather and synthesize user evidence, develop a theory-informed technological solution, and create and evaluate a functional prototype demonstrating one critical user pathway.

docs.title: Ⅱ. Course Objectives
docs.text:
Knowledge After taking class, students will be able to understand the socio-psychological mechanisms and principles underlying how people engage with media and information technologies; explain how the distinctive affordances of different media shape user experience and possible design outcomes; and critically examine intended effects and unintended consequences on individuals and and society as a whole, including their ethical issues in technology design.

Skills Be able to connect everyday media-use experiences to theoretical explanations and concepts covered in class, and apply social/psychological principles to the design of technology based on the insights darwn from scientific user research.

Attitudes Approach technology design with curiosity, ethical awareness, and respect for user well-being and autonomy; and participate responsibly and constructively in collaborative project work.

docs.title: Ⅲ. Course Format
docs.text:
• Lectures
  • Class Discussion
  • Design-thinking activities and project workshops
  • Team project presentations

The semester project will be developed progressively during class. Teams will maintain a shared Project Process Folder containing interview materials, affinity maps, ideation records, scenarios, task flows, prototype materials, and feedback records. Workshop artifacts may be submitted as Miro exports, photographs, diagrams, screenshots, or other appropriate formats.

docs.title: Ⅴ. Course Policies
docs.text:
Communication

The instructor aims to respond to e-mails within 48 hours on weekdays. Students are responsible for checking Cybercampus and e-mail regularly for course announcements and updates.

Late Work

Assignments are due at the specified date and time. Late work will be accepted only when an extension has been discussed with the instructor in advance, such as in cases of illness or emergency. Work submitted late without prior communication may receive no credit.

Academic Honesty and AI Use

Plagiarism, self-plagiarism, data fabrication, collusion, and cheating are serious violations of academic integrity and will be addressed according to university policy. Generative AI may be used when specifically permitted for brainstorming, research support, and prototyping. Students remain responsible for the accuracy, originality, and intellectual contribution of submitted work and must disclose AI use as instructed. Fabricated user evidence, interview data, sources, or testing results are prohibited.

Teamwork

All team members are expected to contribute throughout the project. Individual contribution statements and confidential peer evaluations may be used to assess individual participation in team deliverables.
